title: SAGE: A Unified Framework for Generalizable Object State Recognition with S

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The algorithm states: 'We enforce that at least half of the selected concepts are shared. Specifically, to select k concepts, we first select the top-ranked shared concepts until floor(k/2) are selected... In practice, we select the top 5 concepts... and ensure that at least 3 of them are shared.' For k=5, floor(k/2)=2, so the procedure guarantees only 2 shared concepts, not the required 3 (at least half of 5).

It says the states for 'slicing lemon' include 'whole lemon,' 'slicing lemon,' and 'sliced lemon.' This makes the transitioning state identical to the action name; elsewhere (Figure 1, Appendix B) the same state is called 'lemon under slicing.'

The prompt phrase 'What are the useful visual features to distinguish a {state name} {object name}?' is inconsistent with the actual state names (e.g., 'whole lemon') and object names (e.g., 'lemon'), yielding malformed prompts like 'distinguish a whole lemon lemon.' Appendix B's prompt instead asks to distinguish the three state names directly.

The text cites 'Menon and Vondrick, 2022', but the reference list entry is 'Sachit Menon and Carl Vondrick. 2023. Visual classification via description from large language models.' The citation year is incorrect.

The paper cites 'goal completion (Deng et al., 2020)'; the cited Deng et al. 2020 paper is 'Self-supervised 6D object pose estimation for robot manipulation', which is about pose estimation, not goal completion. This appears to be a misattribution.

'Prior work (Souček et al., 2022, 2024; Xue et al., 2024) trains separate specialized models for different objects or actions' contradicts Section 4.1, which states that MTC (Souček et al., 2024) is a unified model for all objects and actions.

predicted_errors.error_location: Tables 6, 7, and A9 vs Section 4.1/Appendix A
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 4.1 explicitly renames the old 'action precision' metric to 'Trans. Pre@1' to avoid confusion, but Tables 6, 7, and A9 continue to use the header 'Action Pre@1' for the same transition-state metric.

The ablation bullet is titled 'Viterbi Temporal Decoding', but Table 5 labels the corresponding ablation 'W/o Dynamic State Locating'. No component called 'Dynamic State Locating' is described in the method.

Appendix D says it evaluates statistical significance of 'our main experiments in Table 6', but Table 6 is the VLM-robustness table, not the baseline comparison. The p-values in Table A9 correspond to the Table 7 comparisons.

The paper claims SAGE 'can perform consistently better' than SOTA and 'significantly outperforms all baselines on novel objects', but Table A9 gives a non-significant p=9.3e-2 for SAGE vs VidOSC on HowToChange F1 novel, and Table 7 contains exact ties on seen F1 and ChangeIt Trans Pre@1. The claims overstate the evidence.

The text says 'while baseline models require the privileged information of actions and objects as inputs', but Table 1 lists MTC as a baseline with no privileged information (✗✗). The statement is only true for specialist baselines, not all baselines.

The paper introduces novel-object and novel-action evaluation but never specifies how the novel splits are constructed, how many objects/actions are held out, or whether the LLM-constructed SAGE graph contains the test-time novel states/actions during evaluation. This is essential for reproducibility and for interpreting open-world results.

The concept-ranking formula uses Z_f, which in Section 3.1 denotes the output of the temporal Transformer, but graph refinement is performed before that model is trained. The notation appears to conflate the trained frame representations with the frozen VLM visual embeddings used for refinement.

Section 3.1 says the input is encoded by a 'pre-trained, frozen vision encoder', but Section 4.1 says the CLIP ViT-L-14 is 'fine-tuned with the pseudo labels and videos from HowToChange' and then used as the vision backbone. The paper does not clarify whether the frozen encoder is the original CLIP or a separately fine-tuned CLIP, or what the fine-tuning protocol was.
